messages.subject: Estimating survival CJS with robust design and primary periods unevenly spaced
messages.subject_clean: Estimating survival CJS with robust design and primary periods unevenly spaced
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone!
                     I'm using a JAGS code to estimate survival using CJS. Main problem (from my naive perspective) is the model in the simplest version estimates two parameters, phi and p, but primary periods are not evenly spaced. For instance, the distance between primary period 1 and 2 can be 3 months and between 2 and three one month.
I would like to estimate, let's say annual survival, but as it is now I guess is somehow averaging over periods right?
I guess a fix would be to get an estimate of survival for each transition between sampling periods and then use the delta method, but I wonder if there is an easier way to deal with unevenly spaced primary periods. I would appreciate your feedback on this!

Here I include a brief description of my model:

model {

    phi ~ dunif(0, 1)         # Prior for survival
    p ~ dunif(0, 1)           # Prior for detection/recapture

    # Likelihood
    for (i in 1:nind){
    # Define latent state at first capture
    z[i,f[i]] <- 1                      #latent state is 1 the year it was captured
    for (k in (f[i]+1):nyear){          #Survival is only modeled after the first year and state process defined only for primary periods
    # State process
    z[i,k] ~ dbern(mu1[i,k])
    mu1[i,k] <- phi * z[i,k-1]
    mu2[i,k] <- p * z[i,k]
    # Observation process
    for (j in 1:nrep){                #I here add a loop to account for secondary periods
    y[i,j,k] ~ dbern(mu2[i,k])

    } #j
    } #k
    } #i
    }

messages.body_plain:
Hi Erica,

In our upcoming AHM2 book, we have a Bayesian implementation of a point pattern model as a Bernoulli GLM with offset equal to the log of the pixel area, when you discretize space into very small units such that each contains ideally at most 1 point (see Baddeley et al. 2010, Electronic Journal of Statistics). This works pretty well, presumably unless you have much more than 10,000 pixels.

Best regards  --- Marc

Yep, you got it.  Difftime (or whatever you want to call it) is a vector of length k, or length = number of intervals over which it is possible to transition.
The values correspond to the duration of the interval: if, say there is a one week interval between the end of primary period 1 & start of 2, and a 20 week interval between end of 2 and start of 3, difftime[1] = 1 ( or 7 days), and difftime [2] = 20 (140).

assume k starts at 2).

Yeah, if the interval between each primary period is different, survival will be different for each interval, although it's just a single parameter (having each phi[length k] vary in some non-constant fashion might fit better]).

John

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am trying to replicate Table 10.3 in Section 10.8, Goodness-of-fit, since the code is not included in the online companion (any suggested code is welcome).  I want to make sure that I understand exactly how Kery and Royle aggregated over columns and rows: a simple sum across rows or columns for the observed and expected values?

My results are slightly different but that could just be due to random error. As an example, here are my results and some code showing how I calculated the first row of Table 10.3:
#                        Chi2 on Cells         Chi2 on Rows         Chi2 on Columns     MB Test
# This sim:   0.68 (0.03-0.95) 0.11 (0.00-0.47) 0.00 (0.00-0.88) 0.00 (0.00-0.01)
# Table 10.3:   0.78 (0.30-0.98) 0.18 (0.02-0.81) 0.00 (0.00-0.03) 0.00 (0.00-0.01)

############################### Strong behavioral response (b=2)
########## Chisq Test on Cells and Aggregated data for Strong behavioral response (b=2)
library(AHMbook)
library(unmarked)
library(AICcmodavg)

set.seed(1)

fitstats <- function(fm) {
  observed <- getY(fm@data) #on cells
  expected <- fitted(fm)    #on cells
  hSit <- rowSums(observed) #on rows; aggregate over columns
  fSit <- rowSums(expected) #on rows; aggregate over columns
  hTmp <- colSums(observed) #on columns; aggregate over rows
  fTmp <- colSums(expected) #on columns; aggregate over rows
  chisq <- sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected, na.rm=T) #on cells
  chisqSit <- sum((hSit - fSit)^2 / fSit, na.rm=T) #on rows; aggregate over columns
  chisqTmp <- sum((hTmp - fTmp)^2 / fTmp, na.rm=T) #on columns; aggregate over rows
  out <- c(Chisq=chisq, ChisqSit=chisqSit, ChisqTmp=chisqTmp)
  return(out)
}

stime=Sys.time()

nd=20
pb.fm <http://pb.fm> <- matrix(nrow=nd,ncol=3)
for (d in 1:nd) {

  data <- simOcc(M = 267, J = 3, mean.occupancy = 0.6, beta1 = 0, beta2 = 1, beta3 = 0, mean.detection = 0.3, time.effects = c(0, 0), alpha1 = 1, alpha2 = -1, alpha3 = 0, sd.lp = 0, b = 2, show.plot=F)
  umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(
    y = data$y,
    siteCovs = data.frame(forest = data$forest),
    obsCovs = list(elev = matrix(rep(data$elev, data$J), ncol = data$J), wind = data$wind))

  fm <- occu(~elev+wind ~forest, data=umf)

  pb <- parboot(fm, fitstats, nsim=500, report=500)

  pb.fm <http://pb.fm>[d,1] <- sum((abs(p...@t.star[,"Chisq"] - 1) > abs(pb@t0["Chisq"] - 1))/ (1 + 500)) #Pr(t_B > t0)
  pb.fm <http://pb.fm>[d,2] <- sum((abs(p...@t.star[,"ChisqSit"] - 1) > abs(pb@t0["ChisqSit"] - 1))/ (1 + 500)) #Pr(t_B > t0)
  pb.fm <http://pb.fm>[d,3] <- sum((abs(p...@t.star[,"ChisqTmp"] - 1) > abs(pb@t0["ChisqTmp"] - 1))/ (1 + 500)) #Pr(t_B > t0)

}

(evalTime = difftime(Sys.time(),stime)) #Time difference ~10s/dataset * 20 = 3 min.

########## MB Test on Det. History Cohorts for Strong behavioral response (b=2)
stime=Sys.time()

set.seed(1)

nd=20
mb.gof.test.fm <http://mb.gof.test.fm> <- NULL
for (d in 1:nd) {

  data <- simOcc(M = 267, J = 3, mean.occupancy = 0.6, beta1 = 0, beta2 = 1, beta3 = 0, mean.detection = 0.3, time.effects = c(0, 0), alpha1 = 1, alpha2 = -1, alpha3 = 0, sd.lp = 0, b = 2, show.plot=F)
  umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(
    y = data$y,
    siteCovs = data.frame(forest = data$forest),
    obsCovs = list(elev = matrix(rep(data$elev, data$J), ncol = data$J), wind = data$wind))

  fm <- occu(~elev+wind ~forest, data=umf)
  mb.gof.test.fm <http://mb.gof.test.fm>[d] <- mb.gof.test(fm, nsim = 100, plot.hist = F, report = NULL, parallel = TRUE)$p.value

} #d

(evalTime = difftime(Sys.time(),stime)) #Time difference ~45s/dataset * 20 = 15 min.

########## output to compare to AHM
Table10.3 <- matrix(nrow=2,ncol=4)
Table10.3[1,1] <- "Chi2 on Cells"
Table10.3[2,1] <- paste0(
  round(median(pb.fm <http://pb.fm>[,1]),2),
  " (",
     round(min(pb.fm <http://pb.fm>[,1]),2),
  "-",
     round(max(pb.fm <http://pb.fm>[,1]),2),
  ")")

Table10.3[1,2] <- "Chi2 on Rows"
Table10.3[2,2] <- paste0(
  round(median(pb.fm <http://pb.fm>[,2]),2),
  " (",
     round(min(pb.fm <http://pb.fm>[,2]),2),
  "-",
     round(max(pb.fm <http://pb.fm>[,2]),2),
  ")")

Table10.3[1,3] <- "Chi2 on Columns"
Table10.3[2,3] <- paste0(
  round(median(pb.fm <http://pb.fm>[,3]),2),
  " (",
     round(min(pb.fm <http://pb.fm>[,3]),2),
  "-",
     round(max(pb.fm <http://pb.fm>[,3]),2),
  ")")

Table10.3[1,4] <- "MB Test"
Table10.3[2,4] <- paste0(
  round(median(mb.gof.test.fm <http://mb.gof.test.fm>),2),
  " (",
     round(min(mb.gof.test.fm <http://mb.gof.test.fm>),2),
  "-",
     round(max(mb.gof.test.fm <http://mb.gof.test.fm>),2),
  ")")

Dear colleagues,

from 13 to 17 January 2020, we will teach a Bayesian Population Analysis workshop at the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach, Switzerland; please see here for info:  http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewtopic.php?f=8&t=3853&sid=075b03e54a7c0b6aca9287fdd3fb3f3f

Brief description of the contents:

In the course we introduce many key models used in the analysis of distribution, abundance and survival, as well as their spatial and temporal patterns, in a Bayesian analysis framework. We closely follow our book “Bayesian population analysis using WinBUGS” (Academic Press, 2012), which will be handed out for free. We use the "industry-standard" programs R and JAGS to fit and understand some of the most widely used models for the analysis of animal and plant populations. These include:
• GLMs and generalized linear mixed models (e.g., Link and Sauer 2002)
• Closed-population models for population size
• Cormack-Jolly-Seber models for survival probabilities
• Multistate capture-recapture models for survival and transition rates
• Site-occupancy models (MacKenzie et al. 2002, 2003) for the analysis of species distributions
• Binomial mixture models (Royle 2004) for the analysis of distribution and abundance with full accounting for observation error
• Integrated population models (Besbeas et al. 2002; Schaub & Abadi 2011)

Thanks for forwarding to people whom you think might be interested.

messages.subject: Autologistic Occupancy Parameterization
messages.subject_clean: Autologistic Occupancy Parameterization
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was curious of peoples experiences with dynamic (multiseason) occupancy models in WinBUGS/JAGS/NIMBLE or even in Stan. In particular, how important is the auto logistic parameterization (see Royle and Dorado 2008 book cap 9) vs the direct colonization/survival parameterization of Royle and Kery 2007 and used in Kery and Schaub (2012)? The model will have covariates and random effects although I’m fairly indifferent to modeling them on psi vs. gamma and phi in terms of inference for this project. The auto logistic parameterization has advantages in terms of MCMC performance but is more difficult to interpret and messier to code. I just don’t know how important the MCMC performance really is or if it’s just a matter of a bit longer chains with the simpler, direct parameterization. Does the posterior get estimated just as well without having to run for 10x or 100x or 1000x times as long?

Thanks for any insights,
Dan
